planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new growth emerges bronze with a fine red picotee edge before maturing to dark green, so give it a spot where that seasonal color show is visible.

directions: Selected for unusually dense flowering, this cultivar packs its leaf axils so tightly toward the branch tips that a single cluster can carry up to fifty tubular yellow florets, producing a far showier and longer summer-into-fall bloom display than the species already in this dataset. New foliage opens bronze-tinted with a thin red picotee margin before settling to deep green, then turns reddish-purple in autumn. Like other bush honeysuckles it spreads gradually by root suckers into a tidy colony and tolerates heat, humidity, and average to dry soils with little care once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; this Sierra Nevada endemic naturally grows along seeps and streambanks, so it needs steadier moisture than most other wild gingers in this dataset and struggles in soils that dry out during summer.

directions: Restricted in the wild to moist meadow edges and stream margins of California's high Sierra Nevada, this species forms a low, dense evergreen mat of rounded, heart-shaped leaves noticeably shorter and finer-textured than the taller, more upright western wild ginger already in this dataset. Its small cup-shaped flowers are an unusual bicolor, deep red on the outside and creamy white within, tucked at soil level beneath the foliage in spring. Because it comes from consistently wet mountain habitats, it is markedly less drought-tolerant than most other Asarum species and is best reserved for a reliably damp shaded spot near a downspout, streamside planting, or bog garden edge.
sources: Jepson eFlora, University of California Berkeley
Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in shade; this species comes from rocky, high-elevation forest sites in the Klamath-Siskiyou region, so sharper drainage than typical wild-ginger habitat helps prevent winter crown rot.

directions: Confined in nature to a narrow band of the Klamath-Siskiyou mountains and adjacent southern Cascades, this wild ginger is prized for heart-shaped, leathery leaves overlaid with striking silvery-cream marbling, a patterned foliage effect the plain deep-green western wild ginger already in this dataset entirely lacks. Small three-lobed flowers, dark greenish-brown outside and reddish within, open flush with the soil surface in spring, mostly hidden beneath the leaves. It spreads slowly by rhizome into an evergreen groundcover mat and, coming from rocky mountainside habitat, tolerates leaner, better-drained shaded sites than most other Asarum species.
sources: Oregon Flora Project, Oregon State University
Native Plants of the Pacific Northwest (pnwflowers.com)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; this Mid-Atlantic native is naturally found on ravine slopes and streambanks in rich hardwood forest and prefers similarly cool, evenly moist conditions in cultivation.

directions: Native to ravine slopes and streambanks from the Mid-Atlantic into the southern Appalachians, this species holds smaller, stiffer, more distinctly mottled leaves than the closely related southern wild ginger already in this dataset, with a rounder overall leaf shape rather than a pronounced arrowhead outline. Its two-inch, leathery, three-lobed flowers range from dark purple to crimson-bronze and open from early spring into early summer, later than most other wild gingers here. Slow to spread, it forms a low, tidy evergreen groundcover best suited to a cool, richly organic woodland bed rather than open or drier shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection grows more slowly than the straight species, so avoid overcrowding it with faster-spreading groundcovers while it establishes.

directions: Selected at Callaway Gardens in Georgia, this cultivar carries noticeably smaller, rounder leaves with heavier, more contrasty silver-white mottling than the straight species already in this dataset, giving individual leaves an almost painted look. It blooms earlier than most Asarum, opening purple-brown, ground-hugging flowers in late winter rather than spring. Slower growing and more mat-forming than typical shuttleworthii, it suits a shaded rock garden edge or small-scale woodland container planting better than use as a fast groundcover.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or young container trees in spring in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind that can shred the huge compound leaves.

directions: A large East Asian understory tree closely related to the Japanese angelica tree already in this dataset, this species is best told apart by its flower cluster, which carries an elongated main axis with shorter-stalked side branches rather than the more evenly branched, umbrella-like flower head of elata. Its stout trunk also tends to carry fewer and smaller prickles than the densely spiny elata, making it a somewhat less hazardous plant to site near paths. Huge, twice-compound leaves up to three feet long give it a bold, tropical presence in a partly shaded border, and plumes of small white flowers in late summer are followed by black berries favored by birds.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Plant young divisions or container stock in spring into deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full to light shade, and choose the final site carefully since its extensive fleshy roots resent being disturbed once mature.

directions: Native to the Himalayan foothills from Kashmir to Nepal, this arching perennial matches the scale of American spikenard already in this dataset but carries much longer, more open flower panicles, sometimes exceeding a foot, made up of small creamy-white blooms that ripen into glossy maroon-black berries. Its large pinnately divided leaves color richly to crimson and purple in autumn rather than simply fading, adding a season of interest the green-persisting American spikenard lacks. Give it deep, reliably moist soil, since lower leaves drop first if the ground dries out, and site it where it can remain undisturbed for years once its fleshy root system settles in.
